DistilBERT-base · Toxic Comment Classification (Fine-tuning)¶

COMP6713 Group Project — Part C: Pre-trained Model + Fine-tuning

This notebook fine-tunes distilbert-base-uncased on our cleaned 6w (~80k) toxicity-labelled comment dataset for binary toxicity classification (0 = non-toxic, 1 = toxic).

What this notebook does (plain English)¶

  1. Loads the lightly-cleaned train / val / test splits and runs a leakage check plus a token-length analysis.
  2. Tokenises the text with DistilBERT's WordPiece tokenizer (handles sub-words, punctuation, casing).
  3. Fine-tunes distilbert-base-uncased with a classification head for 3 epochs.
  4. Uses class-weighted cross-entropy because the dataset is imbalanced (~91% non-toxic / ~9% toxic).
  5. Performs validation-set decision-threshold tuning so the operating point is not stuck at 0.5.
  6. Evaluates on (a) the held-out test set and (b) our own new_200.csv manual-annotation set.
  7. Performs qualitative error analysis — inspects the worst false negatives / false positives.
  8. Saves the fine-tuned model + tokenizer + a JSON of all metrics + plots, ready for the report and the demo.

Why DistilBERT-base?¶

  • A distilled version of BERT-base (66M vs 110M parameters, ~40% smaller, ~60% faster) with ~97% of the original GLUE performance — a strong accuracy / efficiency trade-off for a moderation system that has to scale.
  • Fits comfortably on a free Colab T4 GPU; whole pipeline finishes in ~30 minutes.
  • Light cleaning preserves casing / punctuation so the WordPiece tokenizer can exploit them.

Runtime¶

  • Hardware: Colab T4 GPU (free tier)
  • 3 epochs × ~80k training samples ≈ 30–35 minutes total.

2.1 Quick EDA — class balance & text length¶

Two facts decide our hyper-parameters:

  • Class imbalance → motivates the class-weighted loss in section 4.
  • Token-length distribution → motivates max_length. We picked 128 (covers ~84.5% of training samples; p95 = 241, p99 = 714). Larger windows cost a lot of memory for the long-tail samples.

3. Tokenisation¶

We use the official distilbert-base-uncased tokenizer (WordPiece, lowercased).

Hyper-parameter Value Reason
max_length 128 covers ~84.5% of comments without truncation; halves GPU memory vs 256
truncation True longer comments get tail-cut
padding dynamic via DataCollatorWithPadding pad to longest sample per batch — large speed-up
In [6]:
MODEL_NAME = "distilbert-base-uncased"
MAX_LENGTH = 128
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME)

def to_hf(df):
    return Dataset.from_pandas(
        df[["cleaned_text", "toxic"]].rename(columns={"toxic": "labels"}),
        preserve_index=False,
    )

raw_ds = {"train": to_hf(train_df), "val": to_hf(val_df), "test": to_hf(test_df)}

def tokenize_batch(batch):
    return tokenizer(batch["cleaned_text"], truncation=True, max_length=MAX_LENGTH)

tokenized_ds = {
    split: ds.map(tokenize_batch, batched=True, remove_columns=["cleaned_text"])
    for split, ds in raw_ds.items()
}
tokenized_ds["train"]

4. Handling class imbalance — class-weighted loss¶

Toxic comments are only ~9% of the data. With ordinary cross-entropy the model would minimise loss simply by always predicting non-toxic → ~91% accuracy but ~0% recall on the class we actually care about.

We therefore weight each class inversely to its frequency so that mistakes on the rare toxic class are punished more strongly. This is mathematically equivalent to over-sampling but does not slow down training and is simpler than focal loss.

In [7]:
y_train = train_df["toxic"].values
class_weights_np = compute_class_weight(
    class_weight="balanced", classes=np.array([0, 1]), y=y_train
)
CLASS_WEIGHTS = torch.tensor(class_weights_np, dtype=torch.float32, device=DEVICE)
print("Class weights (non-toxic, toxic):", CLASS_WEIGHTS.tolist())

Class weights (non-toxic, toxic): [0.550948275862069, 5.406937394247039]

5. Custom Trainer and metric function¶

WeightedLossTrainer overrides compute_loss to use the class weights computed above. Everything else (gradient accumulation, fp16, eval loop) is inherited from Hugging Face's Trainer.

The metric function reports accuracy, macro-F1, per-class precision / recall / F1, and we will select the best checkpoint on toxic-class F1 — the metric the assignment cares about most.

In [8]:
class WeightedLossTrainer(Trainer):
    """Trainer that uses class-weighted cross-entropy."""
    def __init__(self, *args, class_weights=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.class_weights = class_weights

    def compute_loss(self, model, inputs, return_outputs=False, **kwargs):
        labels = inputs.pop("labels")
        outputs = model(**inputs)
        logits = outputs.logits
        loss_fct = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=self.class_weights.to(logits.device))
        loss = loss_fct(logits, labels)
        return (loss, outputs) if return_outputs else loss

def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    logits, labels = eval_pred
    preds = np.argmax(logits, axis=-1)
    acc = accuracy_score(labels, preds)
    p_macro, r_macro, f_macro, _ = precision_recall_fscore_support(
        labels, preds, average="macro", zero_division=0)
    p_per, r_per, f_per, _ = precision_recall_fscore_support(
        labels, preds, labels=[0, 1], average=None, zero_division=0)
    return {
        "accuracy": acc,
        "f1_macro": f_macro, "precision_macro": p_macro, "recall_macro": r_macro,
        "f1": f_per[1], "precision": p_per[1], "recall": r_per[1],
        "f1_neg": f_per[0], "precision_neg": p_per[0], "recall_neg": r_per[0],
        "f1_pos": f_per[1], "precision_pos": p_per[1], "recall_pos": r_per[1],
    }

6. Training configuration¶

Hyper-parameter Value Reason
Optimizer AdamW (HF default) standard for transformers
Learning rate 2e-5 safe BERT-family default
Batch size (train / eval) 16 / 32 fits T4 16 GB at max_length=128
Epochs 3 DistilBERT typically converges in 2–3 epochs on this task
Weight decay 0.01 regularisation, HF default
Best-model criterion f1 (toxic-class F1) metric we care about
Eval / save strategy per-epoch small enough to keep all checkpoints
Seeds seed = data_seed = SEED = 42 reproducibility
In [9]:
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_NAME, num_labels=2,
    id2label={0: "non-toxic", 1: "toxic"},
    label2id={"non-toxic": 0, "toxic": 1},
)

training_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir=OUTPUT_DIR,
    num_train_epochs=3,
    per_device_train_batch_size=16,
    per_device_eval_batch_size=32,
    learning_rate=2e-5,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    eval_strategy="epoch",
    save_strategy="epoch",
    save_total_limit=2,
    load_best_model_at_end=True,
    metric_for_best_model="f1",
    greater_is_better=True,
    logging_steps=200,
    report_to="none",
    seed=SEED, data_seed=SEED,
)

data_collator = DataCollatorWithPadding(tokenizer=tokenizer)
trainer = WeightedLossTrainer(
    model=model, args=training_args,
    train_dataset=tokenized_ds["train"],
    eval_dataset=tokenized_ds["val"],
    tokenizer=tokenizer, data_collator=data_collator,
    compute_metrics=compute_metrics,
    class_weights=CLASS_WEIGHTS,
)
print("Trainer ready.")

8. Quantitative evaluation¶

8.0 Decision-threshold tuning on the validation set¶

Class-weighted loss shifts the model's probability distribution, so argmax @ 0.5 is rarely the F1-optimal operating point. We sweep thresholds in [0.10, 0.90] (step 0.05) on the validation set, pick the threshold with the highest toxic-F1, then report both the default-0.5 and the tuned-threshold scores on the test and manual-200 sets.

In [12]:
# threshold sweep on validation set
val_pred = trainer.predict(tokenized_ds["val"])
val_probs = torch.softmax(torch.tensor(val_pred.predictions), dim=-1).numpy()[:, 1]
val_labels = val_pred.label_ids

rows = []
for t in np.arange(0.10, 0.91, 0.05):
    preds = (val_probs >= t).astype(int)
    p, r, f, _ = precision_recall_fscore_support(val_labels, preds,
        labels=[1], average=None, zero_division=0)
    acc = accuracy_score(val_labels, preds)
    rows.append({"threshold": round(float(t), 2), "accuracy": acc,
                 "precision": float(p[0]), "recall": float(r[0]), "f1": float(f[0])})

sweep_df = pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4)
best = sweep_df.loc[sweep_df["f1"].idxmax()]
print(f"Best threshold = {best.threshold:.2f} (val F1 = {best.f1:.4f})")
sweep_df

Best threshold = 0.90 (val F1 = 0.7890)

8.1 On the held-out test set (~10k samples, same distribution as training)¶

Reported at the default 0.5 threshold (drop-in moderation use-case).

In [13]:
def evaluate_at(threshold, dataset, df, split_name):
    pred_out = trainer.predict(dataset)
    probs = torch.softmax(torch.tensor(pred_out.predictions), dim=-1).numpy()[:, 1]
    preds = (probs >= threshold).astype(int)
    labels = pred_out.label_ids
    print(f"\n=== {split_name} (threshold={threshold}) ===")
    for k, v in compute_metrics((pred_out.predictions, labels)).items():
        print(f"  {k:18s}: {v:.4f}")
    print("\nClassification report:")
    print(classification_report(labels, preds, target_names=["non-toxic", "toxic"], digits=4))
    cm = confusion_matrix(labels, preds)
    print("Confusion matrix:\n", cm)
    out = df.reset_index(drop=True).copy()
    out["pred"] = preds; out["prob_toxic"] = probs
    return out

test_results = evaluate_at(0.5, tokenized_ds["test"], test_df, "TEST (6w in-distribution)")

8.2 On the manual annotation set (new_200.csv, 232 comments)¶

This set was hand-labelled and is out-of-distribution — it contains:

  • Real Reddit / YouTube / X comments
  • Sarcasm, attitude shifts, emerging slang
  • ~37.9% toxic ratio (much higher than the ~9% in training data)

Performance here is the honest measure of how the model handles realistic, hard-to-classify content. We use the tuned threshold = 0.9 picked on the validation set.

In [14]:
# fall back to latin-1 because the manual file uses CP1252 quotes
for enc in ("utf-8", "latin-1"):
    try:
        manual_df = pd.read_csv(MANUAL_PATH, encoding=enc)
        print(f"Loaded new_200.csv with encoding={enc}, n={len(manual_df)}")
        break
    except UnicodeDecodeError:
        continue
manual_df = manual_df.dropna(subset=["cleaned_text", "toxic"]).reset_index(drop=True)
manual_df["cleaned_text"] = manual_df["cleaned_text"].astype(str)
manual_df["toxic"]       = manual_df["toxic"].astype(int)
manual_ds = to_hf(manual_df).map(tokenize_batch, batched=True, remove_columns=["cleaned_text"])

manual_results = evaluate_at(0.9, manual_ds, manual_df, "MANUAL_200 (out-of-distribution)")

9. Qualitative analysis — where does the model fail?¶

We look at the most confident wrong predictions in both directions on manual_200:

  • False negatives (FN) — toxic comments the model thought were safe. Often: implicit toxicity, dog-whistles, coded slurs, sarcasm masking aggression.
  • False positives (FP) — non-toxic comments predicted as toxic with high confidence. Often: strong opinions, profanity used non-aggressively, sarcasm, religious / political language.

These categories should be discussed in the report's qualitative analysis section. The full per-error table (with a heuristic error_type column) is saved to manual_200_errors.csv.

In [16]:
def show_errors(results_df, name, top_k=10):
    fp = (results_df[(results_df["toxic"] == 0) & (results_df["pred"] == 1)]
          .sort_values("prob_toxic", ascending=False).head(top_k))
    fn = (results_df[(results_df["toxic"] == 1) & (results_df["pred"] == 0)]
          .sort_values("prob_toxic").head(top_k))
    print(f"\n=== Top {top_k} FALSE NEGATIVES — {name} (model misses real toxicity) ===")
    for _, r in fn.iterrows():
        print(f"  [p_tox={r.prob_toxic:.3f}] {r.cleaned_text[:200]}")
    print(f"\n=== Top {top_k} FALSE POSITIVES — {name} (model wrongly says TOXIC) ===")
    for _, r in fp.iterrows():
        print(f"  [p_tox={r.prob_toxic:.3f}] {r.cleaned_text[:200]}")
    return fp, fn

fp_man, fn_man = show_errors(manual_results, "MANUAL_200", top_k=10)

10. Inference helper for the CLI / demo¶

Once the model is saved to OUTPUT_DIR, downstream teammates can load it via the standard HF pipeline API. We expose a predict() wrapper that respects the tuned threshold = 0.9 picked above so the demo's decision boundary matches the reported numbers.

In [17]:
from transformers import pipeline
clf_pipe = pipeline(
    "text-classification",
    model=OUTPUT_DIR, tokenizer=OUTPUT_DIR,
    device=0 if torch.cuda.is_available() else -1,
    truncation=True, max_length=MAX_LENGTH, top_k=None,
)

def predict(texts, threshold: float = 0.9):
    if isinstance(texts, str):
        texts = [texts]
    raw = clf_pipe(texts, batch_size=32)
    out = []
    for text, scores in zip(texts, raw):
        prob_toxic = next(s["score"] for s in scores if s["label"] == "toxic")
        label = "toxic" if prob_toxic >= threshold else "non-toxic"
        out.append({"text": text, "label": label, "prob_toxic": float(prob_toxic)})
    return out

predict([
    "I love this community, you guys are great!",
    "you are an idiot and should shut up",
    "Not bad, actually pretty interesting take.",
])
Out[17]:
[{'text': 'I love this community, you guys are great!', 'label': 'non-toxic', 'prob_toxic': 0.0021},
 {'text': 'you are an idiot and should shut up', 'label': 'toxic', 'prob_toxic': 0.9987},
 {'text': 'Not bad, actually pretty interesting take.', 'label': 'non-toxic', 'prob_toxic': 0.0084}]

11. Save artifacts¶

All numbers + figures are written to OUTPUT_DIR/ so the report and demo can pick them up:

  • metrics.json — full metrics (val / test, default + tuned thresholds, threshold sweep)
  • manual_200_metrics.json — OOD metrics + confusion matrix
  • manual_200_predictions.csv — every manual-200 row with both default + tuned predictions
  • manual_200_errors.csv — only the wrong rows, with a heuristic error_type for the report
  • training_curves_loss.png, training_curves_f1.png, confusion_matrix.png
  • best_model/ — the fine-tuned weights + tokenizer (~256 MB, kept on Drive only)

Trained-model weights are uploaded to OneDrive: https://unsw-my.sharepoint.com/:u:/g/personal/z5571022_ad_unsw_edu_au/IQDrlt6CZ0h-RoNWbmepSs2KAX5DMChV9hHSwIPqsSUg1F0?e=i0yfXh
